name: Felix Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To begin, describe a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy animal feed, seed, fertiliser and tractor parts for a farm-supplies distributor that serves about eight hundred farms across three counties. I'm up at five, I check the grain and fertiliser prices with an AI assistant I've used every day for two years, and then I ring the mills and the seed houses. Afternoons I drive out to farms, since farmers talk to a man who has mud on his boots. I love that mix of screen and farmyard. What tires me is that fertiliser prices swing wildly and a bad guess costs us a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, fine, a helpful assistant, nothing more. At church I'd say there's a lot of noise about machines, and what matters is that people still work and look after each other. Online I'd say little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be calm. My value is knowing farmers, weather and soil, and no tool does that. My pressure is fertiliser prices, wild swings, and a bad harvest could hit our firm, and then me, as I'm a senior and paid for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep using the assistant for price tracking, and keep visiting farms. I'd save a little more and put some into the small plot of land my brother and I own. I'd keep serving at church on Sundays, it grounds me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a world I know how to live in. There's a steady satisfaction in doing a job well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be calm. What pressure do you still carry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fertiliser prices, mainly. When they spike, farmers delay buying and our cash flow suffers. The firm has cut back twice in my time, and the senior people are not exempt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your day does the assistant already take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a third of it. Price tracking, weather summaries, drafting emails to suppliers. I check each one against what I hear from the farmers, because the data can miss something local.

say: At work I'd call it a **helpful assistant**, nothing more.
At church I'd say what matters is that people still **work** and look after each other.
think: My value is knowing **farmers and weather**, which no tool does, so I feel calm.
My pressure is **fertiliser prices**, and a bad harvest could hit the firm and me.
do: Keep using the **assistant** for price tracking.
Save more and put some into the **plot** my brother and I own.
feel: **Calm**, with steady satisfaction in doing a job well.
S0.quote: My value is knowing farmers, weather and soil, and no tool does that.
fieldNote: He is **calm** because his value is local knowledge, and his pressure is volatile fertiliser prices.
He **checks tool output** against farmers' reports, a habit that suits his adaptive, hands-on style.

steps.text: Use the assistant for price tracking and check it against farmers' reports
Save a bit more and put some into the family plot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say go for it, but keep the human side. At work I'd say let's pilot the tools and look after staff who need training. At church I'd say we should help the young learn a trade as well as a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm in a good spot, because I already use the tools every day. But much of my job is the thinking work on the card, so the team will shrink. The juniors and the ones who won't adapt are the exposed ones, and I'd worry for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the lead on rolling out the tools, so that the firm sees me as someone who makes things work. I'd teach the juniors how to check a machine's work. I'd also start a small advice service for farms on input costs, on the side, using the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of excitement. I like being useful, and I'm confident I can keep up. I'd still feel for those who can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of buying go to software first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Price tracking, tender drafts, routine reorders and demand forecasts. What stays is relationships and the decisions when something odd happens, like a fertiliser shortage. Farmers talk to a man who has mud on his boots, and no software can fake that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do to stay valuable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The advice service would target small farms that can't afford an agronomist. I'd charge a modest fee, work from my own kitchen table, and build up over a few years. It could become my main income when I step back.

say: I'd say **go for it**, but keep the human side.
At church I'd say help the young learn a **trade** as well as a screen.
think: I'm in a good spot because I already use the tools, but **the team will shrink**.
**Juniors** and those who won't adapt are the exposed ones.
do: Take the **lead** on rolling out the tools.
Teach juniors how to **check** a machine's work.
Start a small **advice service** for farms on input costs.
feel: **Calm**, with excitement, and sympathy for those who can't keep up.
S1.quote: Farmers talk to a man who has mud on his boots, and no software can fake that.
fieldNote: He is **adaptive and confident**, and sees a path to an advice business built on his farm contacts.
He feels **sympathy for colleagues** who can't adapt, and aims to teach them.

steps.text: Lead the rollout of the buying tools in my team
Teach juniors how to check a machine's work
Start a small input-cost advice service for farms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a shock and we're not ready. At church I'd say look after each other. At work I'd say the firm must tell us the truth and give notice. Online I'd say whoever builds this should help carry the cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job is mostly done by AI by 2028. I use it daily, so I see how good it is. The robots arrive three years later, and they'd change farms and warehouses. The farm trade would have far fewer people in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd run the numbers with Lucia, cut spending, and ask the firm for a deal on early retirement. I'd launch the advice service early, starting with ten farms I know. I'd also pay off my brother's loan quickly, to free us up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm adaptive, which helps, but four months of savings is thin. I'd feel the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What would you do in the first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Lucia, we've faced hard years before. We'd cut the holiday, sell the second car, and maybe rent the plot. She'd keep her school job, and I'd use my contacts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you speak to Lucia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also tell the juniors the truth in the first month, and help them find something new. A man should say what he sees.

say: I'd say this is a **shock** and the firm must give notice.
I'd say whoever builds this should help carry the **cost**.
think: My job is mostly done by AI by **2028**, and I see how good it is daily.
The robots three years later would change **farms** and warehouses.
do: Run the **numbers** with Lucia and cut spending.
Launch the **advice service** early with ten farms I know.
Ask the firm for an **early-retirement** deal.
feel: **Anxious**, feeling the clock with four months saved.
S2.quote: A man should say what he sees.
fieldNote: He is **anxious but moving fast**, using adaptability to start a business early.
He insists on **telling juniors the truth**, which reflects his straightforward, traditional values.

steps.text: Run the numbers with Lucia and cut spending
Launch the advice service early with ten farms I know
Ask the firm for an early-retirement deal
Sell the second car and consider renting the plot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years and should use them. Fund training in rural areas, support apprenticeships, and do it now. I'd say it to my firm and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years lets me build the advice service and the savings properly. I'd be 63 when it lands. I'd be uneasy rather than anxious, since I have room to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build savings to eight months, finish paying my brother back, and grow the advice service to forty farms. I'd keep my job as long as the firm wanted me, then go part-time by year four. And I'd study some farm-business courses to boost my advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a purpose. It's like a long drive with a storm ahead. You can see it and you can plan the route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years versus two. What does that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take on a role in the firm that shows my worth, like leading a customer data project. People who help bring in change are the last to be let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but modestly. I'd ask a few farmers to try the advice for free, so I'd know what works before charging.

say: I'd say we have a few years and should **use them** for rural training.
I'd say it to my firm and at **church**.
think: Five years lets me build the advice service and **savings** properly.
I'd be **uneasy** rather than anxious, since I have room to move.
do: Build savings to **eight months** and repay my brother.
Grow the advice service to **forty farms**.
Go **part-time** by year four and study farm-business courses.
feel: **Uneasy**, with purpose, like a long drive with a storm ahead.
S3.quote: People who help bring in change are the last to be let go.
fieldNote: He uses the time to **test** and grow the advice service, with free trials first.
His unease is **purposeful**, and he hopes to prove his worth by leading change at the firm.

steps.text: Build savings to eight months and repay my brother
Grow the advice service to forty farms
Lead a customer data project at the firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the next picture, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decade to build something sound: training, apprenticeships, rural support. I'd stay involved at church and with local farm groups.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be 68 and retired, so my worry is for my children and the young buyers. I'd feel I had a decent run and some guilt about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to 62 and retire, run the advice service lightly, and help farms I know. I'd keep using the tools and teach them to my brother. I'd also volunteer with a farm apprenticeship scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for others. Ten years feels like plenty. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is long. What changes in your thinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn a trade or a skill that needs presence, to save young, and to keep their faith and community close. And to use the tools without fearing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd back the apprenticeships most. A young person with hands and judgement will always find work.

say: I'd say a decade lets us build **sound training**, apprenticeships and rural support.
I'd stay involved at **church** and with farm groups.
think: I'd be **68 and retired**, so my worry is for my children and the young.
I'd feel a **decent run** and some guilt.
do: Run the advice service **lightly** and help farms I know.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly for others, and sleeping fine.
S4.quote: A young person with hands and judgement will always find work.
fieldNote: With ten years his concern turns to his **children** and the young, and he backs apprenticeships.
He keeps **a light advice role** after retiring, which suits his curious, hands-on nature.

steps.text: Run the advice service lightly after retiring
Volunteer with a farm apprenticeship scheme

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be too little time to move. I'm adaptive, but I'm 58, we have about four months of savings, and Lucia, my wife, works part-time as a school secretary. What would help is real notice, a fair pension bridge, and rural training schemes that work. I'd like the young to get apprenticeships, not just advice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'd like people to know that adaptable doesn't mean unworried. I use the tools every day, and I still think a man who works hard deserves a fair run.

headlineQuote: Adaptable doesn't mean unworried. I use the tools every day, and I still think a man who works hard deserves a fair run.
portrait: **Felix** is 58, a senior buyer of feed, seed and fertiliser for a farm-supplies distributor serving about eight hundred farms.
He is **curious and adaptive**, uses AI tools every day, and still visits farms in person.
Traditional and pro-market, he values **hard work** and faith, and wants apprenticeships over handouts.
With about **four months saved** and a wife working part-time, his cushion is modest.
He stays calm in slow worlds, but turns **anxious** at a two-year warning, and then plans a rural advice business.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most, since there would be too little time to move and a modest cushion.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **real notice**, a fair pension bridge and rural training that works, plus apprenticeships for the young.
